intro: Every few years the whole economy seems to change its mood at once. Help-wanted signs come down, stores close, and people who still have jobs start worrying about keeping them. Then, sometimes slowly and sometimes fast, the signs go back up. This unit is about that rhythm, the business cycle, and about the biggest tool the national government has for responding to it: the federal budget.

In the first chapter you will name the phases of the cycle, read the indicators forecasters watch, and use aggregate demand and supply to tell a demand shock from a supply shock. You will compare the Great Depression with the recessions of 2007 to 2009 and 2020. You will also see why long-run growth, driven by productivity, skills and technology, matters even more than the cycle over a lifetime.

In the second chapter you will follow a stimulus check through the economy, work out the multiplier, and take apart the federal budget: where the money comes from, where it goes, and why deficits and debt are argued about. You will finish with state budgets, including Illinois's. By the end you should be able to take a real budget proposal, run the numbers, and argue for or against it with the trade-offs named.
bigQuestion: What makes the whole economy rise and fall together, and what can the government's budget do about it, at what cost?

timeline.t: The Sixteenth Amendment allows a federal income tax
The Budget and Accounting Act requires the President to send Congress a yearly budget
The Great Depression begins; the stock market crashes in October
Unemployment peaks near 25%; Congress creates the FDIC to insure bank deposits
The Social Security Act creates old-age benefits and federal-state unemployment insurance
John Maynard Keynes publishes The General Theory, arguing that total demand drives output
The Employment Act commits the federal government to promote maximum employment
The Congressional Budget Act creates the CBO and the modern budget process
A financial crisis deepens the recession; Congress passes a $700 billion rescue program
A stimulus package of roughly $800 billion passes; the recession ends in June
A two-month recession, the shortest on record; the CARES Act sends $1,200 checks

words.d: the repeating rise and fall of total economic activity around its long-run growth path
a significant decline in economic activity that spreads across the economy and lasts more than a few months
a measure that usually changes direction before the overall economy does
total spending on a country's output at each price level: C + I + G + NX
the amount of output produced per worker per hour
the use of federal taxes and spending to influence total output, jobs and prices
more government spending or lower taxes, used to raise aggregate demand in a slump
taxes and benefit programs that raise or lower the deficit on their own as the economy changes
the number of dollars by which total income changes for each dollar of new spending
when government borrowing pushes up interest rates and reduces private investment
the amount by which government spending exceeds revenue in one year
the total amount the federal government owes, built up from past deficits minus past surpluses

test.q: Real GDP rises for three years, levels off for a month, then starts to fall. That turning-point month is the
test.why: The peak is the high point where growth stops and a contraction begins.

test.q: Which data does the recession dating committee weigh most when it picks a peak month?
choices: Payroll jobs, real income, production and sales
The size of the national debt
test.why: The committee dates what actually happened, so it relies on coincident indicators that move with the economy.

test.q: A labor force of 80,000 has 6,400 unemployed people. What is the unemployment rate?
A drought and an oil shortage raise production costs nationwide. What happens in the aggregate demand and supply model?
choices: Aggregate demand shifts right; output and prices rise
Aggregate demand shifts left; output and prices fall
Short-run aggregate supply shifts left; output falls and prices rise
test.why: Higher costs are a supply shock. Firms produce less at every price level, so output falls while prices rise.

test.q: Which statement about the Great Depression is correct?
choices: Unemployment reached about 25% and thousands of banks failed
It began after the FDIC was created
test.why: Unemployment peaked near 25% in 1933, and waves of uninsured bank failures deepened the collapse. Prices fell, not rose.

test.q: At 2% yearly growth, about how many years does it take output to double?
Congress passes a law cutting income taxes during a recession. This is
test.why: A tax cut passed by Congress adds to demand, so it is expansionary fiscal policy. It needed a new law, so it is not automatic.

test.q: With an MPC of 0.6, what is the simple spending multiplier?
Why does a $100 tax cut raise spending less than $100 of government purchases in the simple model?
choices: Households save part of the tax cut before spending any of it
Tax cuts are not counted in GDP
Taxes cannot change during a recession
test.why: The government spends all $100 of a purchase in the first round, but households save part of a tax cut, so the chain starts smaller.

test.q: A worker's income falls from $60,000 to $40,000. Under a tax of 10% on the first $20,000 and 20% above, by how much does her tax bill fall?
Which kind of federal spending is decided each year in appropriations bills?
test.why: Defense is discretionary spending, set each year. The others are mandatory or owed to lenders.

test.q: Debt is $30 trillion and GDP is $30 trillion. Next year the deficit is $1.5 trillion and GDP grows 5%. What happens to the debt-to-GDP ratio?
test.why: Debt becomes $31.5 trillion and GDP becomes $30 × 1.05 = $31.5 trillion, so the ratio stays at 100%.

test.q: Which is an argument made by economists who are less worried about federal debt?
choices: The U.S. borrows in its own currency and at relatively low rates
Interest payments squeeze out other spending
High debt leaves less room in the next emergency
Borrowing can crowd out private investment
test.why: The other three are arguments made by those worried about debt. Borrowing in dollars at low rates is the main reassuring argument.

test.q: Illinois's state income tax is best described as
choices: progressive, with higher rates on higher incomes
flat, with one rate for every taxpayer
test.why: Illinois's constitution requires one rate, 4.95% for individuals since 2017.

test.q: A state's revenue falls $5 billion in a recession and it must balance its budget. Which step works least against federal stimulus?
choices: Raising the sales tax by $5 billion
Drawing on a rainy day fund saved in good years
test.why: Using savings closes the gap without taking spending out of the state's economy during the slump.

write.prompt: A recession has pushed unemployment from 4% to 7%. Congress is weighing a $200 billion package: either $1,000 checks to households or road and bridge repair. Using the multiplier, the lags and the national debt, argue which plan is better, or whether to do neither, and name the trade-offs.
tips: Show a multiplier calculation with an MPC you state, and say why the real number is smaller.
Compare the lags: which money reaches the economy while it is still weak?
Say who gets the money and how much of it they are likely to spend.
Name the cost: the added debt, the interest on it, and what else the money could have done.
